catalog_quote: Vowel syncope as a form of vowel weakening or reduction has been thought to be connected to stress (e.g. Bloomfield 1933/1973). Syncope is observed in weak positions, for example an unstressed vowel may syncopate or a vowel in unfooted syllables (see e.g. Blumenfeld (2006) for different syncope realizations). Although lexical tone and overt stress are reported to co-exist, for instance, in some Mixtec languages in Mexico (e.g. de Lacy 2002 and references therein), the phenomenon is rare in Gur, but suggested at least for Dagaare (see Anttila & Bodomo 2009). In Samue, however, there is no support for overt stress. ... In Samue, only the front high vowel /i/ syncopates. Therefore, the *NUC/i constraint is employed (264). Other constraints needed in syncope analysis are linked to syllable structure, as there is no overt stress in Samue.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Samue is a three-level tone language (H, M, L, lexical and grammatical); the author finds no evidence for (overt) word stress and analyses prosody purely in terms of tone and syllable/mora structure.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the statement is made in passing within the syncope analysis rather than in a dedicated stress section, so it is a negative finding rather than an instrumental demonstration.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology of the Niansogoni (central) dialect; tone chapters treat downdrift/downstep at phrase level but no stress/accent domain is posited.
new_statements.identity_note: Description is based on the Niansogoni (central) dialect of Samue (author distinguishes northern Néguéni/Klani, central Niansogoni/Outourou, southern Sourani); language = Glottolog wara1292 'Samue/Wara', ISO wbf. Author published earlier under the name Virpi Kalliorinne.

sources.note: Samue is analysed as a three-level tone language (H, M, L; lexical and grammatical tone, downstep, M-spreading). No chapter on stress; in the syncope analysis (sec. 6.4.4.2, p.170) the author states explicitly that there is no support for overt stress in Samue and that syncope constraints are therefore tied to syllable structure, not stress.
